newsitem.title: USA: U.S. senator tries to rev up tax talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. senator tries to rev up tax talks.

text.p: Republicans facing a self-imposed deadline for crafting a final tax bill took a step toward the White House's position on Friday in an effort to "get the ball moving," tax negotiators said.

"It was part of our effort to get the ball moving, we don't have that much time," Sen. William Roth, a Delaware Republican, said of a discussion draft he put on the table at a meeting with administration officials and other key congressional tax negotiators.

Roth chairs a House-Senate group trying to work out differences in their respective tax legislation so that a final tax cut bill can go before Congress for a vote. Republican leaders want work completed on the bill by the end of next week so it can be acted on by the full Congress before the August recess.
Some Democrats have questioned whether that was a realistic timetable given the nature of the differences between the Republican bills and White House views.
The tax legislation would implement a part of the May budget agreement between congressional leaders and President Bill Clinton that called for $85 billion in net tax cuts over five years.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican, earlier on Friday said: "I still feel very good about us being able to get agreement in the Congress and then make sure we have an understanding with the administration. We hope to do that early next week."

In the two-hour evening meeting, tax negotiators discussed the major issues -- a $500 per-child tax credit, education incentives, expanded Individual Retirement Accounts, estate tax relief and a capital gains tax cut.
"We just talked about all the major issues," Assistant Senate Majority Leader Don Nickles, an Oklahoma Republican, said. "We had a good discussion, no final decisions were made."
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and White House officials would not comment after the meeting.
"I think Senator Roth made some suggestions that moved significantly in the administration's direction," House Ways and Means Chairman Bill Archer said.
"One of the really constructive things is they did not at any time say 'oh my gosh you can't do that because the president will veto it'," Archer said of the administration officials.
House and Senate tax negotiators this week exchanged offers and reached agreement on some of the more minor issues.

Lott earlier said Republicans would insist a final tax bill include a reduction in the maximum capital gains tax rate to 20 percent from 28 percent. "We feel strongly about the necessity for a significant cut in the capital gains tax rate to 20 ... percent, and we will insist on that in the final package," he said.
